clue.text: Two to go infra dig, perhaps, in play

indicators.note: 'perhaps' says the letters before it are only one possible arrangement, so they may be shuffled into another

parts.note: all fifteen letters of these words are used

explanation.surface: A pair of characters in a play find leaving beneath their dignity.
explanation.walkthrough: Beckett's play has two tramps who keep saying 'Let's go' and never do, so the surface nods at the plot.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Beckett's absurdist drama about Vladimir and Estragon is a celebrated stage work.

clue.text: Play "Of Mice and Men" that he produced to entertain company

indicators.note: to entertain guests is to take them in, so the rearranged letters hold something inside
to produce a show is to put it together and stage it, so the letters are worked into a new form

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
CO is the standard abbreviation for company

explanation.surface: A theatre producer stages Steinbeck's Of Mice and Men to amuse a touring troupe.
explanation.walkthrough: The quoted title looks like the play wanted, but it is only fodder; THE ICEMAN COMETH by Eugene O'Neill is built round CO.
explanation.definitionFit: Eugene O'Neill's drama about drinkers in a New York saloon is a well-known stage work.

clue.text: Swedes, possibly in love, get a blessing

indicators.note: 'in' says the wanted letters sit inside the run of words that follows

parts.note: the letters run across these words, ignoring the comma

explanation.surface: Scandinavians in love receive a benediction, perhaps at their wedding.
explanation.walkthrough: Swedes reads as people from Sweden; a swede is also a root vegetable (rutabaga in America), hence 'possibly'.
explanation.definitionFit: A swede is a yellow-fleshed root crop, one example of the edible plants grown for the kitchen.

clue.text: Kind of strength in numbers — priest overthrown

parts.note: tens are numbers

indicators.note: an overthrown thing is turned upside down, which in a down clue means read from the bottom up

parts.note: Eli is the priest in the Book of Samuel, a crossword regular

explanation.surface: A priest is toppled by strength in numbers, a crowd overpowering one man.
explanation.definitionFit: Tensile strength is the engineering measure of how much pulling force a material resists before breaking.

clue.text: Virtually tax-free star

indicators.note: virtually means almost but not quite, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: free of tax is 'no VAT', value added tax being Britain's sales tax

explanation.surface: A celebrity who pays almost no tax.
explanation.walkthrough: VAT is value added tax, the British sales tax; 'no VAT' loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A nova is a star that suddenly flares to many times its usual brightness before fading.

clue.text: Terribly industrious (can't play)

indicators.note: terribly suggests something badly done, so the letters come out in a scrambled order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: Someone extremely hard-working who simply cannot act or perform.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's bloodiest tragedy, about a Roman general's revenge, is one of his stage works.

clue.text: Play Ankoolger?

parts.note: surface reading: a nonsense word offered as the title of some play
setter's reading: the word for anger has a four-letter word for 'see' written backwards inside it

explanation.walkthrough: The answer describes the clue: LOOK is reversed to KOOL and placed inside ANGER, giving AN-KOOL-GER, hence LOOK BACK IN ANGER, John Osborne's play.
explanation.definitionFit: John Osborne's 1956 drama about an angry young man is a landmark of British theatre.

clue.text: An expensive buy, but it's only money — on the contrary!

parts.note: cash is money
mere means only, as in 'a mere ten pounds'
gives no letters: it says the two words of the phrase before it swap places

explanation.surface: Shrugging off a costly purchase: it's only money.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'it's only money' is not itself the answer; the setter's 'on the contrary' turns it round, a device that reorders whole words rather than letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Cashmere is fine goat wool, a luxury fabric that costs a lot to buy.

clue.text: Singer Roy hasn't a b___ prayer!

indicators.note: lacking a b means that letter is taken out

parts.note: Roy Orbison, American singer of Oh, Pretty Woman

explanation.surface: A jibe that the singer hasn't a hope, with the swear word blanked out.
explanation.walkthrough: The dashes look like a censored 'bloody'; they really say the B is missing.
explanation.definitionFit: Orison is an old literary word for a spoken appeal to God.

clue.text: To make an impact, walk out

definitions.meaning: second meaning: to stop work in protest

explanation.surface: Advice to protesters: to make your mark, down tools and leave.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means both to hit something hard and to withdraw labour in an industrial dispute.

clue.text: Seek disturbance around water such as this?

definitions.text: Seek disturbance around water such as this?

indicators.note: around says the jumbled letters go either side of what follows
a disturbance stirs things up, so the letters before it are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
aqua is Latin for water

explanation.surface: Looking for an upheaval under the ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the answer: a disturbance around water, which is what an earthquake on the seabed is.
explanation.definitionFit: A seaquake is an earthquake whose epicentre is under the ocean floor, shaking the water above.

clue.text: Stake decapitating infernal poet

indicators.note: decapitating cuts off the head, so the first letter goes

parts.note: Dante wrote the Inferno

explanation.surface: A wooden stake used to behead a hellish poet, a gothic horror scene.
explanation.definitionFit: In poker the ante is the bet each player puts in before the deal.

clue.text: A lamb seen frolicking with a sailor

indicators.note: frolicking means leaping about playfully, so the letters jump into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A lamb spotted gambolling alongside a seaman.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'a' before sailor is part of the fodder, not just an article.
explanation.definitionFit: An able seaman is a rating in the navy or merchant fleet, a qualified crew member at sea.

clue.text: Submarine activity seen in Germany in avoidance of duty

indicators.note: the second 'in' says the letters before it go inside the phrase after it

parts.note: skiving is British slang for dodging work or school
taken as written
D is the international vehicle code for Germany

explanation.surface: Something underwater is spotted in Germany by someone shirking their duties.
explanation.walkthrough: Submarine is used literally, meaning under the sea, not a vessel. To skive is British slang for avoiding work.
explanation.definitionFit: Skin diving is swimming under the sea without a full suit, so it is an underwater pastime.

clue.text: A powerful story is pleasant

parts.note: taken as written
F is forte, the musical instruction for loud and strong
a fable is a moral tale

explanation.surface: A gripping tale makes for an enjoyable read.
explanation.definitionFit: Affable describes someone friendly and easy to talk to, a close synonym of agreeable company.

clue.text: Antelopes slide goat backwards

indicators.note: backwards means the words before it are read from right to left

parts.note: to skid is to slide
a kid is a young goat

explanation.surface: Antelopes push a goat back down a slope.
explanation.definitionFit: Dik-diks are tiny African antelopes named for their alarm call.

clue.text: Leaves character, but not the last retiring copper arrested

indicators.note: something arrested is held, so it is taken inside the other piece
the final letter of the word before is to be dropped

parts.note: a character is a letter of the alphabet

indicators.note: retiring means going back, so the word is read upwards

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

explanation.surface: A character leaves, except for the last policeman, who retires after making an arrest.
explanation.walkthrough: Leaves looks like a verb but is the noun: salad leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: Lettuce is a salad plant grown and eaten for its green foliage.

clue.text: Cooked with oil around dish, no part is stewed with a thick white sauce

definitions.text: stewed with a thick white sauce

indicators.note: around says the first piece wraps the second

parts.note: fried food is cooked in oil

indicators.note: the dish loses a word meaning a role in a play

parts.note: a casserole is a dish

explanation.surface: A cooking instruction: fry, then stew in a creamy white sauce.
explanation.walkthrough: A part is a ROLE, removed from CASSEROLE to leave CASSE.
explanation.definitionFit: To fricassee is to cut meat into pieces and simmer it in a creamy white gravy.

clue.text: Pen sound, but able to write?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the noise heard from a pigpen
second meaning, playful: read as '...', a pen that has ink and so can write

explanation.surface: Is the pen in good order, and can it actually write?
explanation.walkthrough: Pen means a writing pen in the surface but a pigsty for the definition; split O-INK, the answer suggests a pen with ink.
explanation.definitionFit: Oink is the grunting noise a pig makes, the sound you hear from a sty.

clue.text: Sneak up to players making an impression on the beach

parts.note: to worm is to creep or sneak
the cast is the players in a show

explanation.surface: Someone creeps up to actors to win their favour on the seaside.
explanation.definitionFit: A wormcast is the coiled heap of sand left on the shore by a burrowing lugworm.

clue.text: Crooked as a grass, we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is a sound, so the spelling goes by pronunciation

parts.note: rye is a cereal grass

explanation.surface: Bent like a blade of grass, so they say.
explanation.walkthrough: Grass suggests an informer, but here it is the plant rye.
explanation.definitionFit: Awry means askew or out of line, the same as bent out of its proper position.

clue.text: Harvey Smith's chevrons?

parts.note: surface reading: stripe markings on a uniform belonging to someone called Harvey Smith
setter's reading: Harvey Smith, a British showjumper, made a famous rude two-finger gesture at judges in 1971; that gesture is shaped like a chevron

explanation.walkthrough: In Britain the two-fingered gesture with the palm inward is an insult; Harvey Smith's 1971 showjumping salute made it famous.
explanation.definitionFit: The rude two-finger salute forms a V shape, which is what a chevron is.

clue.text: Hang around with children's author

definitions.meaning: second meaning: Beatrix ..., who wrote Peter Rabbit

explanation.surface: Spending time in the company of a writer for youngsters.
explanation.definitionFit: To potter is to dawdle about doing little; Beatrix Potter created Peter Rabbit for young readers.

clue.text: Customer in a restaurant?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: anyone who buys goods or services
second meaning, playful: someone found in a restaurant eats up food

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the second meaning as whimsical: a diner literally devours what is served.
explanation.definitionFit: Economists call any purchaser of goods this, and the word also means one who eats or uses up.
